why.correct: Albumin pulls cholesterol from the sperm membrane, and bicarbonate and calcium enter the sperm. These are the changes of capacitation, which makes the sperm able to undergo the acrosomal reaction and fertilize. Swimming alone is not enough.
options: Correct. The medium copies the female tract fluids that capacitate sperm.
The cortical reaction happens in the oocyte after one sperm has fused with it. It blocks further sperm; it does not help any sperm get in.
Sperm finish both meiotic divisions in the testis, long before ejaculation. It is the oocyte that finishes meiosis II at fertilization.
The acrosome forms during spermiogenesis in the testis. These sperm already had one; what they lacked was the ability to use it.

why.correct: Sperm must capacitate before they can fertilize. They then cross the outer layer, the corona radiata, and release their acrosomal enzymes to cross the inner layer, the zona pellucida. Fusion of one sperm starts calcium waves in the oocyte, which trigger the cortical reaction and restart meiosis II. Finally the two haploid pronuclei combine their chromosomes into the diploid zygote.
The zona pellucida is the clear glycoprotein coat lying directly against the outside of the oocyte's plasma membrane, inside the corona radiata.
options: The corona radiata is the outer layer of granulosa cells, outside the zona pellucida.
Correct. This is the zona pellucida, the glycoprotein coat next to the oocyte.
The plasma membrane is the oocyte's own membrane, the thin line just inside the zona pellucida.
The acrosome is part of the sperm head, not a layer around the oocyte.

why.correct: The corona radiata is the outer ring of granulosa cells that left the follicle with the oocyte. Sperm cross it first.
options: Correct. These cells are the corona radiata.
The theca is the outer layer of the follicle wall. It stays in the ovary and becomes part of the corpus luteum.
The zona pellucida is the clear, cell-free coat inside the corona radiata.
Cortical granules are vesicles inside the oocyte, just under its plasma membrane, not a layer of cells outside it.

why.correct: Calcium waves drive two separate outcomes: cortical granule exocytosis and the restart of meiosis II. Blocking only the granules removes the zona block to polyspermy, so more sperm can bind and polyspermy becomes more likely, while meiosis II still finishes.

variables.name: Calcium waves in the oocyte after fusion
variables.why: The calcium waves are set off by the enzyme the sperm delivers. The drug acts on granule fusion, which comes after the calcium rise.

variables.name: Cutting of ZP2 in the zona pellucida
variables.why: The enzyme that cuts ZP2 is released from the cortical granules. If they cannot fuse, it stays inside them.

variables.name: Number of sperm able to bind the zona after the first sperm enters
variables.why: With ZP2 uncut, the zona still offers binding sites, so more sperm keep attaching.

variables.name: Chance of polyspermy
variables.why: The zona block is lost, and only the slower membrane block remains, so a second sperm is more likely to get in.

variables.name: Completion of meiosis II
variables.why: Meiosis II is restarted by the calcium waves, not by the cortical granules, so it still finishes.

why.correct: The needle carries the sperm through the corona radiata, the zona pellucida and the plasma membrane, so the steps for crossing them, including the acrosomal reaction and membrane fusion, are skipped. Once inside, the sperm still has to activate the oocyte with calcium waves, and the oocyte still has to finish meiosis II.
options: Correct. The needle passes through the corona radiata.
Correct. No enzymes are needed to digest a path, so the acrosomal reaction is bypassed.
Not bypassed. The injected sperm still releases its enzyme into the cytoplasm, which starts the calcium waves that activate the oocyte.
Correct. The needle crosses the zona pellucida.
Not bypassed. The oocyte still finishes meiosis II when the calcium waves release its pause.
Correct. The sperm is placed inside, so its membrane never fuses with the oocyte's.

why.correct: Sperm stored in the cervical crypts and the tube's isthmus can survive up to about five days and are released a few at a time. Some were still available when the oocyte arrived after ovulation on day 14.
options: There was no oocyte on day 11; ovulation happened on day 14. Once released, an oocyte lives only 12 to 24 hours.
Correct. Sperm survival of up to about five days is what makes the fertile window about six days long.
Fertilization needs an ovulated secondary oocyte. None existed until day 14.
Sperm do not enter the ovary. Fertilization happens in the ampulla of the uterine tube after the oocyte is released.

why.correct: Every oocyte carries an X chromosome, because the mother is XX. About half of sperm carry a Y, so a Y chromosome in the zygote must have come from the sperm.
options: The mother has no Y chromosome, so no oocyte can carry one.
The second polar body is discarded by the oocyte and holds maternal chromosomes, one of them an X.
Correct. The sperm sets the zygote's genetic sex.
Only the father's gametes can carry a Y. The mother's always carry an X.

why.correct: The ovulated oocyte already finished meiosis I just before ovulation and is paused at metaphase II. Sperm entry releases that pause, so it completes meiosis II.
options: This step is right. The sperm's enzyme triggers repeated calcium release from the oocyte's endoplasmic reticulum.
This step is right. That is the cortical reaction, the zona block to polyspermy.
This is the error. Meiosis I finished before ovulation; the oocyte completes meiosis II after sperm entry.
This step is right. Meiosis II is lopsided, and the discarded set of chromosomes leaves in the second polar body.
This step is right. Each pronucleus holds one set of chromosomes and copies its DNA before the first mitotic division.

why.correct: The acrosomal reaction releases the enzymes that digest a path through the zona pellucida, so it comes just before the sperm crosses it.
options: Correct. The acrosome's enzymes open a path through the zona.
The cortical reaction happens in the oocyte after a sperm has fused, so it comes after the last step shown.
The second polar body forms when the oocyte finishes meiosis II, after sperm entry.
Pronuclei form after sperm entry, as the last stage of fertilization.

why.correct: The block to polyspermy in human eggs works at the zona, where the cortical reaction cuts ZP2 and stiffens the zona, and at the membrane, which loses its sperm-binding receptor protein.
options: Correct. Cut ZP2 can no longer bind new sperm.
Correct. The stiffened zona stops sperm already inside it from advancing.
Correct. Without the receptor protein, sperm that reach the membrane cannot fuse.
The corona radiata cells are being dispersed by sperm, not tightened. The block acts at the zona and the membrane.
The second polar body is a tiny cell holding discarded chromosomes. It does not seal anything.

why.correct: Without an acrosome, a sperm has no enzymes to digest a path through the zona pellucida, however many try or however well they are capacitated. Injecting a sperm into the cytoplasm skips the zona entirely. Round-headed sperm often carry too little of the enzyme that activates the oocyte, so clinics may also add a treatment that raises calcium in the oocyte after the injection.
options: Sperm numbers are already normal. More sperm without acrosomes would fail in the same way.
Every one of his sperm lacks an acrosome, so more of them adds no enzymes. Numbers are not the problem.
Correct. Intracytoplasmic injection skips the zona, the step these sperm cannot pass.
Capacitation readies a sperm to release its acrosome's enzymes. A sperm with no acrosome has nothing to release.

why.correct: Sperm must travel from the uterus through the tube to meet the oocyte in the ampulla. A blockage near the uterus stops them before they reach it. In vitro fertilization works around this by bringing oocytes and sperm together outside the body.
options: Meiosis I finishes just before ovulation, inside the follicle. Tube scarring does not affect it.
The question says she still ovulates. Ovulation is an event in the ovary, not the tube.
Capacitation is a change in the sperm driven by tract fluids. Even if some happened in the uterus, capacitated sperm still could not pass the blockage.
Correct. The blockage separates sperm from oocyte.

why.correct: These are the changes of capacitation. Tract proteins strip cholesterol from the membrane, calcium enters and the tail becomes hyperactivated, which readies the sperm to cross the layers around the oocyte. Its chromosomes do not change.

variables.name: Cholesterol in the sperm's plasma membrane
variables.why: Albumin and other proteins in the tract fluid pull cholesterol out of the membrane.

variables.name: Calcium inside the sperm
variables.why: Calcium enters through the sperm's calcium channels, which open during capacitation.

variables.name: Force of the tail's beat
variables.why: The rise in calcium switches the flagellum to hyperactivated, whip-like beating.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in the sperm
variables.why: Capacitation changes the membrane and the tail. The sperm stays haploid, with 23 chromosomes.

why.correct: The zygote is the product of fertilization: a single cell with 46 chromosomes, 23 from each parent. It divides by mitosis to form every cell of the body.
options: Correct. The zygote is the first diploid cell of a new individual.
The secondary oocyte is the haploid cell released at ovulation, before any sperm has entered.
A capacitated sperm is still a haploid gamete, not the product of fertilization.
That is the second polar body, which breaks down.

why.correct: Two whole paternal sets plus one maternal set means two sperm delivered their nuclei into one oocyte. That is polyspermy, which the cortical reaction and the membrane block normally prevent.
options: Nondisjunction of one pair adds or removes a single chromosome, giving 45 or 47, not a whole extra set of 23.
If the oocyte skipped meiosis I, the extra set would be maternal, not paternal.
Copying DNA twice would double every set equally, maternal and paternal alike, giving 92 chromosomes.
Correct. Two sperm, each with 23 chromosomes, plus the oocyte's 23 gives 69.

why.correct: Human sperm bind the zona pellucida through ZP2. Antibodies covering ZP2 would hide those binding sites, so sperm could not attach to the zona and cross it.
options: Correct. Blocking the sperm-binding glycoprotein blocks attachment to the zona.
Capacitation happens to sperm in the uterus and tube, before they reach the oocyte. Antibodies on the zona would not affect it.
Calcium waves need a sperm to fuse first. The vaccine acts earlier, at the zona, so no sperm would get that far.
Meiosis II finishes after sperm entry. The vaccine would act before any sperm entered.

why.correct: The sperm's midpiece, packed with mitochondria, is drawn into the oocyte at fusion. Within days those paternal mitochondria are tagged and broken down, so only the oocyte's mitochondria survive.
options: Correct. Paternal mitochondria enter but are destroyed.
Sperm do have mitochondria: they fill the midpiece and power the tail.
The midpiece enters the oocyte along with the nucleus at membrane fusion.
Mitochondria come only from existing mitochondria, which divide. They carry their own DNA and cannot be built from scratch.

why.correct: hCG is secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast, which forms only as the blastocyst invades the endometrium from about day 6 to 7. hCG reaches the mother's blood in measurable amounts about 8 to 10 days after fertilization, so a test on day 5 is too early.
options: The corpus luteum does not make hCG; it responds to it. hCG comes from the embryo's trophoblast.
Correct. No implantation means no syncytiotrophoblast and no hCG in her blood.
The heart starts beating around day 22, long after hCG first appears. hCG depends on implantation, not on the heart.
A day-5 embryo is not secreting hCG at all. Secretion begins with the syncytiotrophoblast during implantation.

why.correct: Cleavage divides the zygote into blastomeres and then a solid morula. Fluid pumped into the morula forms the blastocoel of the blastocyst, which must hatch from the zona pellucida before it can attach. Once attached, the trophoblast forms the invading syncytiotrophoblast, which begins secreting hCG.
The inner cell mass is the cluster of cells against the inside of the trophoblast at one end of the blastocyst. It forms the embryo.
options: The trophoblast is the single outer layer of flat cells that surrounds the whole blastocyst.
The blastocoel is the fluid-filled cavity, not a cluster of cells.
Correct. This cluster is the inner cell mass.
The morula is the earlier solid ball of cells, not a part of the blastocyst.

why.correct: The trophoblast is the outer layer of flat cells around the blastocyst. It attaches to and invades the endometrium and forms supporting tissues, not the embryo.
options: Correct. This outer layer of cells is the trophoblast.
The zona pellucida is a cell-free glycoprotein coat, which the blastocyst sheds when it hatches.
The inner cell mass is the cluster of cells inside the blastocyst, at one end.
The epiblast forms later, in week 2, as one layer of the disc made from the inner cell mass.

why.correct: hCG keeps the corpus luteum alive. With too little of it, the corpus luteum dies, progesterone falls and the endometrium is shed, ending the pregnancy. This is one way a very early pregnancy is lost, often before it is recognized.

variables.name: Survival of the corpus luteum past its usual two weeks
variables.why: Without enough hCG acting on its LH receptor proteins, the corpus luteum dies on its usual schedule.

variables.name: Progesterone in the mother's blood
variables.why: The dying corpus luteum stops making progesterone, and the embryo's own tissues cannot yet make enough.

variables.name: Chance that the endometrium is shed
variables.why: Falling progesterone sets off menstruation, and the functional layer, with the embryo in it, is shed.

variables.name: Intensity of a home pregnancy test line
variables.why: The test detects hCG in urine, so less hCG gives a fainter line or a negative result.

why.correct: Mesoderm forms all three kinds of muscle, the dermis, bone and cartilage, blood and vessels, the heart and the kidneys. Ectoderm forms the epidermis, and endoderm forms the lining of the digestive tract.
options: Correct. Skeletal muscle comes from the myotomes of the somites, which are mesoderm.
The epidermis comes from ectoderm, the outer germ layer.
Correct. The dermis comes from mesoderm, including the dermatome part of each somite.
The epithelium lining the stomach comes from endoderm, which forms the gut tube.
Correct. The heart muscle forms from mesoderm.
Correct. Bone, and the cartilage models it replaces, come from mesoderm.

why.correct: The sclerotome of each somite forms the vertebrae and ribs. A defect confined to one sclerotome would leave a malformed vertebra and rib at that level, while the muscles (from the myotome) and the dermis (from the dermatome) develop normally.
options: The myotome forms skeletal muscle. The question says the back muscles are normal.
The neural crest forms peripheral ganglia, Schwann cells and some head tissues, not vertebrae or ribs.
The apical ectodermal ridge drives limb growth. It has no role in the vertebrae or ribs.
Correct. The sclerotome forms vertebrae and ribs.

why.correct: The pancreas buds from the foregut, a tube of endoderm, so its ducts and the cells lining them come from endoderm. Its connective tissue and blood vessels come from mesoderm.
options: Ectoderm forms the epidermis, the nervous system and a few other structures, not the lining of gut glands.
Mesoderm forms the pancreas's connective tissue and vessels, not the epithelium lining its ducts.
Correct. Epithelium of the gut and the glands that bud from it comes from endoderm.
Neural crest forms peripheral ganglia and Schwann cells, among other things, but not pancreatic duct epithelium.

why.correct: hCG resembles LH, not FSH. It binds LH receptor proteins on the cells of the corpus luteum, which is what keeps the corpus luteum alive.
options: This step is right. The syncytiotrophoblast is the source of hCG.
This is the error. hCG acts like LH, on the corpus luteum.
This step is right. hCG rescues the corpus luteum from its usual death.
This step is right. The rescued corpus luteum keeps making progesterone.
This step is right. Progesterone maintains the endometrium, so no period comes.

why.correct: The ridge keeps the mesoderm under it dividing, so the limb grows from its tip, laying down parts from the body outward. Parts already formed stay; parts not yet formed never grow. Removing it after the upper part has formed leaves a limb cut short beyond that point.
options: Without the ridge, the mesoderm under it stops being driven to divide. The instructions it provides are needed until the whole limb has formed.
The upper wing had already formed when the ridge was removed, so it remains.
Correct. Growth stops at the level reached when the ridge was removed.
Limbs grow from the body outward. A tip cannot form without the parts nearer the body, and here the tip had not yet formed.

why.correct: The blastocoel forms because the outer cells pump sodium into the center and water follows by osmosis. Blocking the pumps blocks that fluid collection, so the morula cannot become a proper blastocyst, even though its cells keep their normal chromosomes.

variables.name: Sodium pumped into the center of the morula
variables.why: The outer cells use sodium–potassium pumps to move sodium inward. Blocked pumps move less.

variables.name: Water moving into the center
variables.why: Water follows the solute. With less sodium collecting in the center, less water enters.

variables.name: Size of the blastocoel
variables.why: The blastocoel is the fluid that collects in the center. Less water in means a smaller cavity or none.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in each blastomere
variables.why: The drug blocks ion pumping, not DNA copying or mitosis. Each cell stays diploid.

why.correct: The primitive streak is the midline groove in the epiblast through which cells move during gastrulation to form the endoderm and mesoderm.
options: The notochord is a rod of mesoderm under the ectoderm, formed by cells moving forward from the head end of the streak. It is not where cells pass down.
Correct. Cells pass through the primitive streak during gastrulation.
The neural tube forms after gastrulation, from ectoderm folding up along the back.
The hypoblast is the lower layer of the two-layered disc, which the first cells through the streak replace.

why.correct: The amnion is the thin inner membrane that surrounds the embryo and encloses the amniotic cavity and its fluid.
options: The chorion is the outer membrane, next to the endometrium and the maternal blood.
The yolk sac hangs from the embryo's belly side and holds no amniotic fluid.
The allantois is a small outpouching into the stalk that ties the embryo to the chorion.
Correct. The amnion encloses the amniotic fluid around the embryo.

why.correct: hCG is made by the syncytiotrophoblast, and the trophoblast forms the chorion. The hormone's name records this: chorionic gonadotropin.
options: The amnion forms from epiblast, not trophoblast, and does not make hCG.
Correct. The chorion's syncytiotrophoblast secretes hCG.
The yolk sac forms from hypoblast. Its wall makes the first blood cells, not hCG.
The allantois is a small outpouching whose vessels become the cord's vessels. It does not make hCG.

why.correct: Later in pregnancy, most amniotic fluid is fetal urine, so no kidneys means almost no fluid. The lungs need fluid breathed in and out, and room to expand, to grow. Without it they stay small, and the baby cannot breathe adequately after birth.
options: Correct. Too little amniotic fluid stunts lung growth.
Vertebrae form from sclerotomes in the first weeks, before the kidneys make urine. Missing fluid does not remove them.
The neural tube closes by about day 28, well before urine forms the fluid. Its closure does not depend on the kidneys.
Fingers are freed by apoptosis in weeks 6 to 8. Little fluid can press on the limbs, but it does not remove the fingers.

why.correct: The morula becomes a blastocyst when fluid collects inside it. The blastocyst is the stage that hatches and implants.
options: Gastrulation happens in week 3, after implantation, in the embryonic disc.
Correct. The blastocyst follows the morula and implants.
The two-layered embryonic disc forms from the inner cell mass during implantation, in week 2.
The neural tube closes in week 4, long after implantation.

why.correct: Limb buds appear near the end of week 4 and their parts form over the following weeks. A drug that disrupts limb formation can only do so while it is happening. By week 12 the limbs are already formed, so the same drug no longer causes that defect.
options: The blastocyst hatches from the zona pellucida in its first week. There is no zona around a fetus.
The difference follows the embryo's stage of development, not a change in the mother's handling of the drug.
Correct. Organs are most easily damaged while they are forming, during weeks 3 to 8.
Many drugs still reach the fetus after week 8. What changes is which structures are still forming.

why.correct: A synovial joint cavity opens when the cells in the middle of the interzone die. If they survive, no cavity forms, and the two bones stay joined by tissue instead of moving freely against each other.
options: Correct. Without the cells dying, no cavity opens.
A synovial joint needs a cavity. The cells that should die are the ones that make room for it.
Extra digits come from extra ridges in the limb's hand or foot plate, not from the knee's interzone.
The length of a bone depends on its growth, not on whether a joint cavity forms beside it.

why.correct: Cells at the edges of the neural folds become the neural crest. They break away as the neural tube closes and migrate to form, among other things, the neurons of the ganglia outside the CNS and the Schwann cells.
options: The cerebral cortex forms from the neural tube itself, not from the crest cells at its edges.
The lining of the gut forms from endoderm.
Vertebrae form from the sclerotomes, which are mesoderm.
Correct. Neural crest cells form peripheral ganglia and Schwann cells.

why.correct: The foregut forms the pharynx, esophagus, stomach and first part of the duodenum, and the liver, pancreas and the lining of the airways bud from it. The rectum and the bladder lining come from the hindgut.
options: Correct. The esophagus is foregut.
Correct. The stomach is foregut.
The rectum forms from the hindgut.
Correct. The lining of the larynx, trachea and lungs buds from the foregut.
The lining of the urinary bladder comes from the hindgut region.
Correct. The pancreas buds from the foregut.

why.correct: The syncytiotrophoblast is the outer layer of the trophoblast: a single mass of cytoplasm with many nuclei and no cell boundaries. It digests its way into the endometrium and secretes hCG.
options: The cytotrophoblast is the inner trophoblast layer of separate cells, next to the blastocyst cavity.
Correct. This invading multinucleated mass is the syncytiotrophoblast.
The endometrium is the mother's tissue that the syncytiotrophoblast invades.
The hypoblast is the lower layer of the embryonic disc, not part of the trophoblast.

why.correct: Both limbs start out pointing the same way. In weeks 7 and 8 the arms rotate outward, turning the elbows back, and the legs rotate inward, turning the knees forward and the big toes to the medial side.
options: Correct. Opposite rotations of the limbs set their final orientation.
Both pairs of limb buds bulge from the sides of the body wall.
The orientation is set before birth, by the rotation in weeks 7 and 8.
Both joints form from mesoderm, through the same kind of joint interzone.

why.correct: The placental barrier lets small, uncharged or fat-soluble molecules through and holds back large, highly charged ones. Warfarin crosses and can harm the developing fetus; heparin stays in the mother's blood.
options: The placenta does break down a few substances, but heparin is kept out by its size and charge, not destroyed.
Warfarin works in pregnant women. The concern is that it crosses to the fetus.
Heparin does not cross in useful amounts, and the fetus does not need an anticoagulant.
Correct. Its size and charge keep heparin on the mother's side.

why.correct: The hCG curve climbs steeply from about week 4, peaks at week 10 and then falls to a low plateau by about week 18.
options: At week 4 hCG is only starting to rise from zero.
Correct. The hCG peak sits at week 10.
By week 24 hCG has fallen to about 15% of its peak.
At week 40 hCG is low. It is progesterone and estrogens that peak at the end.

why.correct: A placenta that receives too little maternal blood delivers less oxygen and fuel. The fetus grows slowly, protects its brain by redirecting blood, and its kidneys, receiving less, make less urine, so the amniotic fluid shrinks. A small fetus with little amniotic fluid is the classic pattern.

variables.name: Oxygen reaching the fetal blood
variables.why: Less maternal blood in the intervillous space means a smaller supply of oxygen at the villi, so less diffuses into fetal blood.

variables.name: Fetal growth rate
variables.why: Less glucose and fewer amino acids reach the fetus, so it grows more slowly.

variables.name: Share of fetal blood flow going to the brain
variables.why: Low oxygen makes the fetus narrow vessels to its kidneys, gut and limbs and redirect blood toward its brain and heart.

variables.name: Fetal urine output
variables.why: With blood diverted away from them, the fetal kidneys filter less and make less urine.

variables.name: Amniotic fluid volume
variables.why: Late in pregnancy, most amniotic fluid is fetal urine, so less urine means less fluid.

why.correct: Chorionic villi are the branching projections of the chorion that hang in the pool of maternal blood. Each contains fetal capillaries in a connective tissue core.
options: Correct. These branching projections are the chorionic villi.
The uterine arteries are the mother's vessels in the uterine wall, which feed the intervillous space.
The amnion is the thin membrane lining the fluid-filled sac around the embryo.
The umbilical cord is the single rope-like stalk joining the embryo to the placenta.

why.correct: Vessels are named by the direction of flow relative to the heart. The umbilical vein returns blood from the placenta toward the fetal heart, so it is a vein even though its blood is rich in oxygen, just as the pulmonary veins are.
options: Veins are defined by direction of flow, not by valves, and the umbilical vein is not named for them.
Correct. It carries blood toward the heart.
Its wall is thinner, but wall thickness does not define an artery or a vein.
Its pressure is low, but pressure does not decide the name. Direction does.

why.correct: The rate of diffusion is proportional to area × partial pressure difference ÷ distance. New rate ÷ old rate = (1/2 × 1) ÷ 2 = 1/4.
options: Both changes slow diffusion, so the rate cannot stay the same.
One-half accounts for the smaller area but not for the doubled distance.
Correct. Half the area and twice the distance give one-quarter of the rate.
One-eighth would need a third halving. Only two factors changed, each by a factor of 2.

why.correct: Small, uncharged or fat-soluble molecules such as oxygen, carbon dioxide and alcohol diffuse through the membranes of the barrier down their gradients. Glucose needs carrier proteins, amino acids are actively transported, and IgG is carried across in vesicles.
options: Correct. Oxygen diffuses down its partial pressure gradient.
Glucose crosses by facilitated diffusion, through carrier proteins.
Correct. Alcohol is small and fat-soluble, and it diffuses freely.
IgG is too large to diffuse. It is carried across by receptor proteins in vesicles.
Correct. Carbon dioxide diffuses from fetal to maternal blood.
Amino acids are pumped to the fetus by active transport, against their gradients.

why.correct: hCG was needed to keep the corpus luteum making progesterone. By weeks 7 to 9 the placenta makes enough progesterone itself, and the progesterone curve keeps rising while hCG falls. Progesterone, not hCG, keeps the endometrium in place.
options: A fall in hCG does not act on the uterus. It is progesterone that keeps the endometrium from being shed.
The corpus luteum depends on hCG, so it does not grow as hCG falls. After weeks 7 to 9 it is simply no longer needed.
Correct. The placenta has taken over progesterone production.
hPL acts mainly on the mother's metabolism and the breasts. It does not keep the corpus luteum alive.

why.correct: Glucose crosses the placenta down its gradient by facilitated diffusion, so high maternal glucose means high fetal glucose. Maternal insulin does not cross, so the fetal pancreas answers the high glucose by secreting more of its own insulin, which also drives extra growth.
options: Glucose carriers move glucose down its gradient, so a higher maternal level pushes more across. The placenta does not cap it.
Insulin is a protein too large to cross the placenta in useful amounts.
Her low insulin raises her own glucose, and that extra glucose crosses to the fetus. Fetal glucose rises, not falls.
Correct. Fetal glucose follows maternal glucose, and the fetal pancreas responds.

why.correct: Graves disease antibodies are IgG, which the placenta actively carries to the fetus. They stimulate the fetal thyroid as they do the mother's. After birth no more arrive, and the ones present are broken down over weeks to months, so the condition fades.
options: The baby's problem is driven by stimulation of its own thyroid, and it lasts as long as the maternal antibodies do, not by stored hormone.
The condition fades as the borrowed antibodies disappear, which rules out a lifelong disease of the baby's own immune system.
Correct. Borrowed IgG antibodies stimulate the baby's thyroid until they are cleared.
The placenta does not make thyroid hormone. The goiter shows the baby's own thyroid being stimulated.

why.correct: Receptor proteins on the syncytiotrophoblast carry IgG across, and most of the transfer happens late in pregnancy. A baby born at 28 weeks misses much of it and has less passive immunity.
options: Newborns, especially preterm ones, make antibodies poorly. They depend on borrowed IgG.
IgG is carried in vesicles, not by diffusion, and its transfer does not depend on the lungs.
Correct. Most IgG transfer happens in the last three months.
Birth does not destroy IgG. The preterm baby simply received less of it.

why.correct: Maternal blood bathes the outside of the villi. It never enters the fetal capillaries: the placental barrier separates the two bloods, and substances cross it instead.
options: This step is right. The spiral arteries are branches of the uterine arteries.
This step is right. The spiral arteries open into the intervillous space.
This is the error. The two bloods do not mix; maternal blood stays outside the villi.
This step is right. Oxygen crosses the barrier by diffusion.
This step is right. Blood leaves the intervillous space through the uterine veins.

why.correct: Less carbon dioxide means fewer hydrogen ions in the fetal blood, which raises hemoglobin's affinity for oxygen: the Bohr effect in reverse. At the same time, the maternal blood gains carbon dioxide and releases more oxygen. Together this is the double Bohr effect.
options: A right shift happens when carbon dioxide rises, as in the fetus's own tissues, not when it falls.
Fetal hemoglobin shows the Bohr effect like adult hemoglobin. It is its weak binding of 2,3-BPG that differs.
The maternal side does shift right and release more oxygen, but the fetal side's own left shift also increases loading. Both sides contribute.
Correct. Losing carbon dioxide shifts the fetal curve left, so it takes up more oxygen.

why.correct: Oxygen enters the mother's blood in her lungs, travels in her arteries to the spiral arteries and into the intervillous space, crosses the placental barrier into the fetal capillaries of the villi, and returns to the fetus through the umbilical vein before reaching the fetal tissues.

The placenta takes over progesterone production from the corpus luteum by about weeks 7 to 9. By 12 weeks, the corpus luteum can be removed without ending the pregnancy. Removed before about week 7, it would need to be replaced with progesterone.
options: A corpus luteum forms only from a follicle after ovulation. It does not regrow, and ovulation does not happen in pregnancy.
hCG acts on the corpus luteum, not on the endometrium. With the corpus luteum gone, hCG has nothing to act on.
Correct. The placenta supplies the progesterone.
Progesterone is needed throughout pregnancy. It keeps the endometrium in place and the uterine muscle quiet.

why.correct: The umbilical cord is the rope-like stalk joining the embryo to the placenta. It holds two umbilical arteries and one umbilical vein.
options: The chorionic villi are the branching projections in the enlarged view, not the rope-like stalk.
The yolk sac is a small sac near the top of the embryo in this drawing, not the stalk to the placenta.
Correct. This is the umbilical cord.
The allantois is a small early outpouching whose vessels become the cord's vessels. By this stage the cord has formed.

why.correct: Of these hormones, human placental lactogen makes the mother's cells respond less to insulin. A placental growth hormone, progesterone and cortisol add to the effect. Her glucose stays higher after meals, and more of it crosses to the fetus. hPL rises with the size of the placenta, so the effect is strongest late in pregnancy.
options: Correct. hPL reduces the mother's response to insulin.
hCG peaks near week 10 and then falls, so it does not explain an effect that grows late in pregnancy.
Relaxin peaks early in pregnancy and acts mainly on blood vessels and the kidneys.
Estriol grows the uterus and breast ducts. It is not the main cause of the mother's reduced insulin response.

why.correct: Under the syncytiotrophoblast lies a layer of cytotrophoblast cells, which becomes patchy later in pregnancy as the barrier thins.
options: The amnion lines the fluid-filled sac around the fetus. It is not part of the villi.
Correct. The cytotrophoblast lies under the syncytiotrophoblast.
The endometrium is the mother's tissue around the intervillous space, not a layer inside the villus.
The uterine epithelium was eroded where the syncytiotrophoblast invaded. It is not a layer of the villus.

why.correct: A normal cord holds two umbilical arteries, carrying oxygen-poor blood to the placenta, and one umbilical vein, carrying oxygen-rich blood to the fetus.
options: This reverses the numbers. There are two arteries and one vein.
Correct. Two arteries and one vein.
There is only one umbilical vein in a normal cord.
A cord with a single artery is an uncommon finding that prompts a closer look for other problems.

why.correct: Remodeling replaces the muscle of the spiral arteries so they become wide, low-resistance tubes. Arteries that keep their muscle stay narrow and can still constrict, so resistance stays high and flow into the intervillous space is lower. This is the usual starting point of placental insufficiency.
options: Failed remodeling does not break down the placental barrier. The bloods still stay apart.
Correct. High resistance means low flow to the placenta.
Fetal hemoglobin production is set by the fetus's own genes and age, not by the spiral arteries.
Arterial smooth muscle sets the vessel's width; it does not pump blood. Narrower arteries carry less.

why.correct: At week 30, hPL is at about 70% of its peak, higher than progesterone (about 60%) and estrogens (about 50%). hPL rises with the size of the placenta and levels off from about week 36.
options: hCG is at only about 15% of its peak at week 30.
Progesterone is at about 60% of its peak at week 30, below hPL.
Estrogens are at about 50% of their peak at week 30 and rise most steeply at the end.
Correct. hPL's curve is highest at week 30.

why.correct: Normally left atrial pressure is higher, which keeps the septum primum flap pressed shut over the foramen ovale. Straining briefly raises right atrial pressure above left. The flap swings open toward the left, and a clot arriving in the right atrium can cross into the left atrium and travel to the brain.
options: Higher left atrial pressure presses the flap shut. The flap opens only when right atrial pressure is higher.
The ductus arteriosus closes permanently soon after birth and does not reopen with straining. The opening involved is between the atria.
Clots in the lungs lodge in the pulmonary arteries; they do not pass through by speed. This clot bypassed the lungs through the atrial opening.
Correct. The pressure difference reverses and the one-way flap opens right to left.

why.correct: Blood takes the path of lower resistance. The fetal lungs are filled with fluid, and low oxygen narrows their vessels, so their resistance is high. The ductus arteriosus is a wide channel into the aorta, whose pressure is kept low by the placenta.
options: The pulmonary valve only stops backflow into the right ventricle. It does not steer blood.
The fetal lungs do receive some blood, about a tenth to a quarter of both ventricles' output together. The question is why the rest goes elsewhere.
Correct. Flow follows the lower resistance, into the ductus.
The ductus has smooth muscle that can narrow it, but it does not pump. Pressure differences drive flow through it.

why.correct: Oxygen-rich blood leaves the placenta in the umbilical vein, partly bypasses the liver through the ductus venosus, enters the inferior vena cava and right atrium, and is aimed through the foramen ovale into the left atrium. The left ventricle pumps it into the ascending aorta, whose first branches supply the heart and head.
The ductus arteriosus is the short channel between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta. It carries most of the right ventricle's output past the lungs.
options: The ductus venosus lies at the liver and links the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava.
The foramen ovale is an opening in the wall between the atria, inside the heart.
Correct. This channel from the pulmonary trunk to the aorta is the ductus arteriosus.
The umbilical vein runs from the placenta through the cord to the liver.

why.correct: The ductus venosus carries oxygen-rich blood from the umbilical vein straight to the inferior vena cava, bypassing the liver.
options: Correct. This shunt at the liver is the ductus venosus.
The ductus arteriosus is near the heart, between the pulmonary trunk and the aorta.
The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the gut into the liver. The pinned vessel goes past the liver instead.
The inferior vena cava is the large vein the ductus venosus empties into, not the shunt itself.

why.correct: Prostaglandins hold the ductus arteriosus open. Blocking them late in pregnancy narrows it, so pressure rises in the right ventricle and pulmonary trunk and more blood is forced through the high-resistance lungs. The same drug lowers fetal urine output across another system, shrinking the amniotic fluid. That is why such drugs are avoided late in pregnancy.

variables.name: Prostaglandin levels acting on the ductus arteriosus
variables.why: Ibuprofen crosses the placenta and blocks the enzyme that makes prostaglandins in the fetus and placenta.

variables.name: Diameter of the ductus arteriosus
variables.why: Prostaglandins keep the ductus's smooth muscle relaxed. Without them it contracts and narrows.

variables.name: Pressure in the fetal pulmonary trunk and right ventricle
variables.why: The narrowed ductus resists the right ventricle's outflow, so pressure builds up behind it.

variables.name: Blood flow through the fetal lungs
variables.why: With the ductus narrowed, more of the right ventricle's output is forced into the pulmonary arteries.

variables.name: Amniotic fluid volume
variables.why: Prostaglandins also help keep fetal kidney blood flow up. Blocking them lowers fetal urine output, which is most of the amniotic fluid late in pregnancy.

why.correct: The umbilical vein carries blood straight from the placenta, where it picked up oxygen, at about 80% saturation. Everywhere else, it has mixed with oxygen-poor blood or given up oxygen to tissues.
options: The umbilical arteries carry blood back to the placenta after the fetal tissues have taken oxygen from it. They have the lowest saturation of these.
The pulmonary trunk carries mostly oxygen-poor blood from the head and arms, pumped by the right ventricle.
The descending aorta carries a mix, including oxygen-poor blood from the ductus arteriosus.
Correct. The umbilical vein carries the freshest blood from the placenta.

why.correct: The ductus venosus lets blood bypass the liver. The foramen ovale lets blood bypass the right ventricle and lungs, and the ductus arteriosus lets the right ventricle's output bypass the lungs. The shunts deliver blood to the left ventricle, the brain and the placenta; they do not route blood around them.
options: Correct. The ductus venosus carries part of the umbilical blood past the liver.
Correct. Both the foramen ovale and the ductus arteriosus route blood around the lungs.
Blood crossing the foramen ovale goes into the left ventricle, so no shunt bypasses it.
The shunts send the best-oxygenated blood to the brain. They do not bypass it.
Correct. Blood crossing the foramen ovale skips the right ventricle.
The umbilical arteries carry blood to the placenta. No shunt bypasses it.

why.correct: Her Sertoli cells work normally and secreted anti-Müllerian hormone before birth, so the paramesonephric ducts, which would have formed the uterus and uterine tubes, broke down. Because no tissue responds to androgens, her mesonephric ducts also broke down and her external genitalia developed as female.
options: Correct. Anti-Müllerian hormone acts without androgen receptor proteins, so the uterus never formed.
The uterus comes from the paramesonephric ducts, not the mesonephric ducts.
The uterus forms from ducts, not from the ovaries. She has testes, which removed those ducts before birth.
Her testosterone cannot act on her cells at all, and the uterus was absent from before birth.

why.correct: Anti-Müllerian hormone from the Sertoli cells normally makes the paramesonephric ducts break down. If it is missing or cannot act, those ducts survive and form a uterus and tubes, while testosterone still keeps the mesonephric ducts and DHT still makes the external genitalia male.
options: Testosterone worked, since his mesonephric ducts formed a normal ductus deferens.
DHT worked, since his external genitalia are male.
Correct. Without anti-Müllerian hormone, the paramesonephric ducts persist.
hCG drives the fetal Leydig cells to make testosterone. His testosterone-dependent structures are normal, so hCG action was adequate.

why.correct: The truncus arteriosus is the outflow end of the heart tube, at the head end. A spiral wall later splits it into the ascending aorta and the pulmonary trunk.
options: The sinus venosus is the inflow end, where the veins drain in, at the tail end of the tube.
The bulbus cordis is the next region in from the outflow end. It becomes most of the right ventricle.
The primitive atrium lies toward the inflow end, between the ventricle and the sinus venosus.
Correct. The outflow end is the truncus arteriosus.

why.correct: The sinus venosus, the inflow chamber the veins drained into, is absorbed into the back wall of the right atrium. It forms the smooth part of that wall, the coronary sinus and the region of the SA node, which is why the node is named for it.
options: The bulbus cordis forms most of the right ventricle and the outflow parts of both ventricles.
Correct. The sinus venosus forms the smooth back wall of the right atrium, where the SA node sits.
The truncus arteriosus forms the ascending aorta and pulmonary trunk.
The primitive ventricle forms most of the left ventricle.

why.correct: The heart tube starts beating at about day 22 after fertilization, before it loops and long before the septa finish dividing it. It is the first organ to work.
options: This step is right. The cardiogenic area forms around day 18.
This step is right. The cords hollow into paired endocardial tubes.
This step is right. Side-to-side folding brings the tubes together to fuse around day 21 to 22.
This is the error. The tube beats from about day 22, well before the chambers are divided.
This step is right. Looping and septation follow in weeks 4 to 7.

why.correct: The cardiogenic cords hollow out into two endocardial tubes, which fuse into the primitive heart tube.
options: Correct. The paired endocardial tubes come between the cords and the single tube.
Blood islands are clusters of hemangioblasts that form vessels and blood cells, not the heart tube.
Endocardial cushions form later, inside the looped tube, and divide the canal between atrium and ventricle.
The septum primum forms later still, when the atria are divided.

why.correct: After birth, left ventricular pressure is much higher than right, so oxygen-rich blood is pushed from left to right through the hole. That extra blood recirculates through the lungs and overloads them, causing fast breathing, but it does not send oxygen-poor blood to the body, so the skin stays pink.
options: Correct. Left-to-right flow overloads the lungs but does not cause cyanosis.
After birth, the lungs' resistance falls far below its fetal level, so right-sided pressures become lower than left.
The direction is left to right, but because the left ventricle generates the higher pressure, not the right.
Right-to-left flow would send oxygen-poor blood into the aorta and cause cyanosis, which this baby does not have.

why.correct: In the first two weeks after fertilization, before the germ layers form, an exposure usually either ends the pregnancy or does no lasting harm, because the few cells can replace damaged ones. Limb buds do not appear until near the end of week 4.
options: Limb defects need exposure while the limbs are forming, from about week 4 to week 8 after fertilization.
Poor growth comes from exposures in the fetal period. This exposure was far earlier.
Organs are not yet forming on day 10, so the drug has no heart or limb tissue to disrupt.
Correct. Before week 3, the effect is usually all or none.

why.correct: Rubella virus crosses the placenta and damages the eye, inner ear and heart while they form, early in pregnancy. The classic trio is cataracts, deafness and heart defects, among them a patent ductus arteriosus.
options: Correct. Cataracts, deafness and heart defects go together in congenital rubella.
Extra fingers and cleft lip are not the typical pattern of rubella.
Rubella tends to cause a small head and poor growth, not overgrowth.
Absent kidneys cause too little amniotic fluid, not too much, and are not typical of rubella.

why.correct: The trachea grows as a bud from the front of the foregut, and a wall of tissue normally separates it from the esophagus behind. If the separation is incomplete, an abnormal connection lets milk from the esophagus pass into the trachea.
options: Poor branching would leave small lungs, but it would not let milk into the airway.
Correct. Incomplete separation leaves a connection between the esophagus and trachea.
The olfactory pits form the nasal cavities. A problem there would not link the esophagus to the trachea.
Too little surfactant makes the lungs stiff, but it does not cause choking on feeds.

why.correct: At 27 weeks the lungs are between the canalicular and saccular stages. Type II cells are present, but they usually make enough surfactant only by weeks 34 to 36. Without it, surface tension collapses the alveoli, making the lungs stiff. A glucocorticoid given to the mother before the birth would have sped surfactant production.
options: The pseudoglandular (branching) stage ends around week 17. By 27 weeks respiratory bronchioles and early air sacs have formed.
Correct. Too little surfactant makes preterm lungs stiff.
The ductus venosus carries blood past the liver. It does not affect how stiff the lungs are.
Early closure of the foramen ovale would strain the fetal right heart before birth. It would not make the lungs stiff.

why.correct: Fetal breathing movements move small amounts of fluid in and out of the airways. Together with the fluid the lungs secrete, they keep the lungs stretched, and that stretch drives lung growth. No gas exchange happens in the fetal lungs.
options: The fetus gets all its oxygen across the placenta. The lungs exchange no gas before birth.
Carbon dioxide leaves the fetus across the placenta, not through the lungs.
Correct. The movements and lung fluid stretch the lungs, and stretch drives their growth.
The ductus arteriosus carries blood driven by the right ventricle. Breathing movements do not pump it.

why.correct: Quickening is when a pregnant woman first feels the fetus move, usually around weeks 16 to 20 of pregnancy, a little earlier in later pregnancies.
options: The heart begins beating about day 22 after fertilization, weeks before anyone can feel movement.
Lanugo is the fine hair that covers the fetus from about mid-pregnancy.
Viability, about weeks 22 to 24, is when a baby born can sometimes survive with intensive care.
Correct. Quickening is the first felt movement.

why.correct: At 30 weeks, the fetus has not yet stored much fat, so the skin looks thin and red. Lanugo still covers the body, and vernix caseosa still coats the skin. Both are mostly gone by term.
options: A plump baby with little lanugo and little vernix fits one born at or after term.
At 30 weeks the lungs are not yet mature; surfactant is usually enough only by 34 to 36 weeks.
Correct. Little fat, plenty of lanugo and vernix fit 30 weeks.
Dry, peeling skin and long nails are typical of a baby born after 41 or 42 weeks, once the vernix has gone.

why.correct: In vasculogenesis, hemangioblasts cluster into blood islands, first in the yolk sac wall. Angioblasts at the edge flatten into endothelium, and the cells in the center become the first blood cells. The islands join into vascular tubes, and later vessels sprout from existing ones by angiogenesis.
options: Correct. Blood islands are clusters of hemangioblasts.
Correct. The yolk sac wall has the first blood islands, around day 17.
Correct. Angioblasts form the endothelium.
The first vessels form from scratch in blood islands. The heart tube links up with them; it does not sprout them.
Correct. The center of each island makes the first blood cells.

why.correct: The septum primum is the thin first wall that grows down from the roof of the atrium. Its lower part later acts as the flap over the foramen ovale.
options: The interventricular septum divides the ventricles, lower in the heart.
Correct. This is the septum primum.
The endocardial cushions are pads that divide the canal between atrium and ventricle, not the wall growing down from the atrial roof.
The foramen ovale is the opening between the atria, not a wall.

why.correct: The third trimester runs from week 28 of pregnancy to birth, so week 30 is in it.
options: The first trimester ends at the end of week 13.
The second trimester runs from week 14 to the end of week 27.
Correct. Week 30 is in the third trimester.
Trimesters meet at a set week; there is no gap between them. The third begins at week 28.

why.correct: The heavy uterus can flatten the inferior vena cava against the spine. Less blood returns to the heart, so preload, stroke volume and cardiac output fall, and blood pressure drops. Turning to the left lifts the uterus off the vein.
options: Correct. Less venous return means less preload and less cardiac output.
Pressure on the aorta could lower flow to the legs, but it would not drop her arm blood pressure this way. The key effect is on venous return.
Her heart kept beating; she felt faint because her cardiac output fell. The fast recovery on turning shows a mechanical cause.
Lying flat does not pool blood in the lungs. The problem is blood held back in the lower body.

why.correct: Compressing the inferior vena cava cuts venous return and preload, so stroke volume, cardiac output and blood pressure fall. The baroreceptor reflex speeds the heart, but that does not fully make up for the lost filling, and flow to the placenta falls with the pressure.

variables.name: Venous return to the heart
variables.why: The flattened inferior vena cava carries less blood back from the lower body.

variables.name: Stroke volume
variables.why: Less venous return means less filling and less preload, so by the Frank–Starling mechanism the ventricles eject less.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Cardiac output falls with stroke volume, so pressure falls.

variables.name: Heart rate
variables.why: The baroreceptor reflex senses the fall in pressure and raises sympathetic drive to the SA node.

variables.name: Blood flow to the placenta
variables.why: The spiral arteries cannot constrict, so placental flow follows the mother's blood pressure and falls with it.

why.correct: Pregnancy lowers vascular resistance, which switches on sodium and water retention. The larger plasma volume raises cardiac output and dilutes the red cells. More blood reaches the kidneys, so GFR rises and creatinine falls. Separately, progesterone drives extra breathing, which lowers PCO2.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: The renin–angiotensin–aldosterone system is switched on, so the kidneys keep sodium and water.

variables.name: Hematocrit
variables.why: Plasma rises by 40 to 50% but red cell mass by only 20 to 30%, so red cells are diluted.

variables.name: Cardiac output
variables.why: Stroke volume rises with the larger blood volume, and heart rate rises too.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Progesterone and other signals relax arterioles, and the placenta adds a low-resistance bed.

variables.name: Glomerular filtration rate
variables.why: Renal plasma flow rises by 50 to 80%, so more is filtered.

variables.name: Serum creatinine
variables.why: A higher GFR clears creatinine faster, so its blood level falls.

variables.name: Arterial PCO2
variables.why: Progesterone makes the brainstem more sensitive to carbon dioxide, so minute ventilation rises more than metabolism and more carbon dioxide is breathed off.

why.correct: Before: 72 × 70 = 5,040 mL/min. At 24 weeks: 84 × 80 = 6,720 mL/min. 6,720 ÷ 5,040 = 1.33, a rise of about 33%.
options: 14% is the rise in stroke volume alone (80 ÷ 70). Cardiac output multiplies heart rate and stroke volume, so both rises count.
20% is not the rise in either factor; heart rate rose about 17% and stroke volume about 14%.
50% is at the top of the usual range for pregnancy but does not match these numbers.

why.correct: MAP = CO × TPR. New MAP = 90 × 1.40 × 0.70 = 90 × 0.98 ≈ 88 mm Hg. The fall in resistance slightly outweighs the rise in output.
options: 126 mm Hg counts the 40% rise in cardiac output but ignores the fall in resistance.
108 mm Hg would need a much smaller fall in resistance. With 1.40 × 0.70, the product is just under 1.
Correct. 90 × 0.98 ≈ 88 mm Hg.
63 mm Hg counts the 30% fall in resistance but ignores the rise in cardiac output.

why.correct: Pregnancy raises plasma volume by 40 to 50% but red cell mass by only 20 to 30%. She has more red cells than before, but they are more diluted, so the concentration falls. A hemoglobin down to about 11 g/dL is expected.
options: Her marrow is making more red cells, driven by erythropoietin. The concentration falls because plasma rises even more.
The fetus does not destroy maternal red cells. Rh disease is the reverse: maternal antibodies against fetal cells.
Maternal and fetal blood do not mix across the placenta, and there is no blood loss through it.
Correct. This is dilutional anemia of pregnancy.

why.correct: Progesterone makes the brainstem more sensitive to carbon dioxide, so minute ventilation rises more than metabolism needs and PaCO2 falls to about 30 mm Hg. The kidneys compensate by excreting bicarbonate, so the pH stays near 7.40 to 7.45. This is the expected pattern in pregnancy.
options: A pH of 7.44 is not acidotic, and the low PaCO2 is the primary change here, not a response to acid.
Correct. This is the normal blood gas of pregnancy.
A raised diaphragm lowers functional residual capacity, but PaCO2 is low, not high. There is no acidosis.
The low bicarbonate shows renal compensation, so it is compensated. The cause is progesterone, which acts in every pregnancy.

why.correct: Scarring from an earlier infection can slow the embryo's trip down the tube, so the blastocyst implants in the tube wall. A positive test with one-sided pain, bleeding, no pregnancy in the uterus and slowly rising hCG points to an ectopic pregnancy, which can rupture as it grows.
options: By 7 weeks with hCG rising, a normal pregnancy inside the uterus is usually visible on ultrasound, and hCG normally doubles every two to three days.
Placenta previa is a placenta over the cervix, a problem of the second half of pregnancy, not of week 7.
The corpus luteum does not make hCG; the trophoblast does. And her hCG is rising.
Correct. This picture fits a tubal ectopic pregnancy.

why.correct: Painless bright red bleeding in the second half of pregnancy suggests placenta previa. A finger in the cervix could push into a placenta lying over it and set off heavy bleeding, so a digital examination is avoided until an ultrasound shows where the placenta is.
options: Vital signs are needed to judge how much blood she has lost. They are safe.
Ultrasound is exactly what finds the placenta's position, and it is safe.
Correct. A digital cervical examination can provoke heavy bleeding from a placenta previa.
An intravenous line prepares for fluid or blood replacement and is appropriate.

why.correct: Preeclampsia begins with a poorly supplied placenta that releases factors blocking vessel growth. They damage the mother's endothelium everywhere: arterioles constrict and pressure rises, capillaries leak and plasma volume falls, the glomeruli filter less and leak protein, and platelets are consumed.

variables.name: Total peripheral resistance
variables.why: Damaged endothelium makes less of the signals that relax arterioles, so they constrict.

variables.name: Mean arterial pressure
variables.why: Pressure is cardiac output times resistance, and resistance has risen.

variables.name: Plasma volume
variables.why: Leaky capillaries let fluid move into the tissues, so less stays in the blood.

variables.name: Glomerular filtration rate
variables.why: The glomerular endothelium swells and narrows the capillaries, so less is filtered.

variables.name: Protein in the urine
variables.why: The damaged filtration membrane lets plasma proteins through.

variables.name: Platelet count
variables.why: Platelets are used up as they stick to damaged endothelium.

why.correct: Before birth, high maternal glucose crossed the placenta, and his pancreas adapted by secreting extra insulin, which also made him grow large. Cutting the cord stopped the glucose supply at once, but his pancreas kept secreting extra insulin for a while, so his glucose fell.
options: Correct. Extra fetal insulin continues after the glucose supply stops.
Type 1 diabetes causes high glucose, not low, and it does not present at birth.
Maternal insulin is a protein too large to cross the placenta.
A newborn's liver does store glycogen late in pregnancy. The problem is the extra insulin.

why.correct: Human placental lactogen and the other hormones that make the mother's cells resist insulin rise with the mass of the placenta, so the resistance is strongest late in pregnancy. That is when beta cells that cannot keep up are unmasked.
options: Fetal insulin does not cross to the mother, and it would lower her glucose, not raise it.
The mother's beta cells multiply in pregnancy. Pressure from the uterus does not shrink the pancreas.
hCG peaks around week 10 and then falls, and it is not the main cause of insulin resistance.
Correct. The resistance grows with the placenta.

why.correct: Progesterone relaxes smooth muscle, which explains the relaxed lower esophageal sphincter, the wider ureters and the slower gut. It also makes the brainstem more sensitive to carbon dioxide, raising ventilation. Estrogens drive the rise in liver clotting factors and the growth of the uterine muscle.
options: Correct. Relaxed sphincter muscle lets acid reflux.
Correct. Progesterone raises the brainstem's sensitivity to carbon dioxide.
Correct. Relaxed ureteral smooth muscle slows urine flow.
Estrogens, not progesterone, make the liver produce more clotting factors.
Correct. Relaxed gut smooth muscle slows transit.
Estrogens mainly drive the growth of the uterine muscle. Progesterone keeps that muscle quiet but does not make it grow.

why.correct: Pregnancy raises GFR by about 50%, so creatinine is cleared faster and a normal pregnant value is lower, often about 0.4 to 0.8 mg/dL. A value of 1.0 suggests her filtration has fallen, for example from preeclampsia.
options: It is the reverse: creatinine falls in pregnancy.
Correct. A higher GFR should bring her creatinine down, so a normal-range value hides reduced filtration.
Creatinine is measured as usual in pregnancy. The issue is reading it against the right range.
The fetus's creatinine is small in amount, and a raised maternal value points to the mother's kidneys.

why.correct: Progesterone relaxes the smooth muscle of the ureters and the uterus presses on them, so they widen and urine moves slowly. Bacteria can climb more easily from the bladder to the kidney against the sluggish flow.
options: Correct. Wide, slow ureters let bacteria climb.
Urine flows down the ureters, however much is filtered. A higher GFR does not push bacteria up.
The main change is in the ureters, not a weakened bladder lining.
Pregnant women usually empty the bladder more often, because the uterus presses on it.

why.correct: At the end of the second trimester, about week 27, the top of the uterus lies a few centimeters above the navel.
options: At the end of the first trimester, the uterus has only just risen out of the pelvis.
Correct. The middle outline, above the navel, marks the end of the second trimester.
At the end of the third trimester, the uterus reaches up toward the bottom of the sternum.
Before pregnancy, the uterus lies entirely in the pelvis.

why.correct: Between weeks 20 and 36, fundal height in centimeters roughly equals the weeks of pregnancy, so about 30 cm is expected. A measurement 8 cm short suggests a small fetus, too little amniotic fluid, or wrong dates, and an ultrasound is needed.
options: A larger fetus would make the fundal height greater than the weeks, not smaller.
At 30 weeks, about 30 cm is expected. 22 cm is well short.
Correct. A low fundal height points to slow growth or low fluid.
Twins would make the uterus larger than expected, not smaller.

why.correct: Damaged endothelium makes fewer of the signals that relax arterioles, so in preeclampsia the arterioles constrict and total peripheral resistance rises. That is what raises the blood pressure.
options: This step is right. Shallow remodeling of the spiral arteries is the starting point.
This step is right. The stressed placenta releases factors that block the growth signals the endothelium needs.
This step is right. The damage is widespread, which is why many organs are affected.
This is the error. The arterioles constrict, so resistance rises.
This step is right. Higher resistance raises pressure, and damaged glomeruli leak protein.

why.correct: A normally placed placenta separating from the uterine wall bleeds behind the placenta, so the bleeding is painful, the uterus is hard and tender, and much of the blood may stay hidden. High blood pressure is a common link. This is placental abruption.
options: Placenta previa bleeds painlessly, with bright red blood and a soft uterus.
Correct. Painful bleeding with a hard, tender uterus is the pattern of abruption.
An ectopic pregnancy is a problem of the first weeks, not of week 35.
Sudden severe pain with bleeding and a hard, tender uterus is never normal.

why.correct: The raised diaphragm lowers her functional residual capacity by about 20%, so she holds less oxygen in her lungs between breaths. At the same time she and the fetus use more oxygen. With a smaller store used faster, her saturation drops sooner.
options: Vital capacity stays about the same in pregnancy.
Tidal volume rises in pregnancy, by about 30 to 50%.
Correct. A smaller reserve and a higher use rate make her desaturate faster.
The mother has adult hemoglobin. The fetus takes oxygen across the placenta, but that is not what empties her lung reserve.

why.correct: Shallow remodeling of the spiral arteries early in pregnancy leaves the placenta short of blood. The stressed placenta releases factors that block vessel growth, which damage the mother's endothelium everywhere. Constricted arterioles raise the blood pressure, and damaged glomeruli leak protein.
More than 95% of ectopic pregnancies implant in a uterine tube, most often in the ampulla.
options: An ovarian pregnancy happens but is rare.
An abdominal pregnancy happens but is rare.
A pregnancy implanted in the cervix happens but is rare.
Correct. The uterine tube is by far the most common site.

why.correct: Irregular contractions that ease with walking and do not change the cervix are false labor. True labor is defined by progressive thinning and opening of the cervix, not by pain.
options: Correct. Irregular timing, easing with activity and no change in the cervix mark Braxton Hicks contractions.
The latent phase is slow, but the cervix does soften, thin and open over time. Hers has not changed at all.
Lightening is the fetal head dropping into the pelvis. It changes breathing and urination, not contractions.
The expulsion stage starts only once the cervix is fully dilated at 10 cm.

why.correct: The drip adds oxytocin to the loop from outside. Contractions strengthen, the head presses harder, the cervix stretches more and sends more signals, and the cervix opens faster. This is why hospitals use oxytocin when contractions are weak.

variables.name: Strength of uterine contractions
variables.why: Oxytocin binds the many oxytocin receptor proteins of the term myometrium and releases calcium inside the cells, so each contraction is stronger.

variables.name: Pressure of the fetal head on the cervix
variables.why: Stronger contractions from the fundus push the head down harder onto the cervix.

variables.name: Afferent signals from the cervix to the hypothalamus
variables.why: More stretch of the cervix fires its stretch-sensitive sensory receptors more.

variables.name: Rate of cervical dilation
variables.why: Stronger contractions and more retraction pull the softened cervix open faster.

why.correct: Stage 1, the dilation stage, runs from true labor to full dilation. Stage 2, the expulsion stage, runs from full dilation through crowning to delivery of the whole baby. Stage 3, the placental stage, ends with delivery of the placenta and membranes, after which firm contraction pinches the placental-bed vessels shut.
Oxytocin is made by hypothalamic neurons and released from their axon endings in the posterior pituitary, not the anterior pituitary.
options: This step is right. The head acts as the wedge that stretches the cervix.
This step is right. The afferent limb of the Ferguson reflex runs from the cervix to the hypothalamus.
This is the error. Oxytocin comes from the posterior pituitary, which is made of hypothalamic axon endings.
This step is right. Oxytocin acts on its receptor proteins in the myometrium.
This step is right. It closes the loop, which is what makes it positive feedback.

why.correct: Prostaglandins are local lipid messengers. They contract the myometrium and ripen the cervix, and oxytocin increases their release.
options: Correct. Prostaglandins strengthen contractions and ripen the cervix.
Progesterone keeps the myometrium quiet. Losing its effect near term frees the uterus to contract; oxytocin does not release it.
Placental CRH rises in the last weeks and helps drive the estrogen changes before labor. Oxytocin does not release it.
Relaxin is a hormone of pregnancy, not a local messenger released by oxytocin during contractions.

why.correct: Labor starts from changes in the uterus itself: gap junctions, oxytocin receptor proteins, prostaglandins, cervical ripening and loss of progesterone's effect. Mice lacking oxytocin or its receptor protein give birth normally, and women with little oxytocin have had normal labors. Oxytocin's loop strengthens contractions; if they are weak, a drip can be given.
options: Oxytocin barely rises before labor. Contractions start from changes in the uterus and placenta, not from oxytocin.
Some textbooks predict a stall, but the evidence shows labor can progress without oxytocin. The loop makes contractions stronger; it is not required.
Correct. Without oxytocin the loop that strengthens contractions is missing, but labor can begin and progress.
Oxytocin makes contractions stronger. Its absence would not speed labor.

why.correct: A positive feedback loop has no set point to return to. It keeps building until an outside event breaks it. Here, birth removes the head from the cervix, the stretch stops and the afferent signals stop.
options: Positive feedback does not settle at a set point; that is how negative feedback behaves.
Progesterone stays high in the blood through labor, and it falls after the placenta is delivered, not before birth. It is not what stops the loop.
The sensory receptors keep firing as long as the stretch lasts. The loop stops because the stretch ends.
Correct. Delivery removes the stimulus, so the loop stops turning.

why.correct: This is uterine atony. The crisscrossing muscle fibers of the upper uterus are the main brake on bleeding from the placental site; when they relax, the vessels stay open. Rubbing the fundus and giving oxytocin make the uterus contract and clamp them.
options: Clotting seals the vessels only after muscle has closed them. A soft, enlarged uterus points to the muscle, not the clotting system.
Correct. Atony leaves the vessels open; firm contraction is what closes them.
Oxytocin makes the myometrium contract, which compresses the vessels. It is the treatment for this bleeding, not the cause.
Early separation would cause bleeding before the birth. Hers began after the placenta was out, with a soft uterus.

why.correct: True labor is defined by progressive change in the cervix, dilation and effacement, and it comes with a regular pattern that builds. Pain and a pattern that fades with rest do not show true labor.
options: Correct. Progressive dilation defines true labor.
Braxton Hicks contractions can also be painful near term. Pain alone does not distinguish them.
Correct. A pattern that becomes more frequent and longer is typical of true labor.
Contractions that stop with rest point to false labor.
Correct. Progressive effacement is a change in the cervix, which marks true labor.

why.correct: Each stage is defined by the event that ends it. The expulsion stage runs from full dilation to the birth of the baby, so a fully dilated woman who has not yet delivered is in it.
options: The dilation stage ends when the cervix reaches 10 cm, which hers has.
The placental stage begins only after the baby is born.
The postpartum period follows delivery of the placenta.
Correct. Full dilation to birth is the expulsion stage.

why.correct: Separation is mechanical. The emptied uterus keeps contracting and shrinks, and the patch of wall under the placenta shrinks with it. The placenta cannot shrink, so it shears off, and blood collecting behind it helps peel it away.
options: Correct. A shrinking wall under a placenta that cannot shrink shears it off.
Oxytocin makes muscle contract. It does not digest tissue.
Progesterone falls after the placenta is delivered, because the placenta makes it. The fall follows separation rather than causing it.
The cord is only a guide once the placenta has separated. Pulling hard on an attached placenta can turn the uterus inside out, which is why clinicians wait for separation.

why.correct: Delivering the placenta removes the hormone source that sustained pregnancy. Hormones fall, the uterus involutes by shrinking its cells, and the kidneys clear the extra fluid of pregnancy.

variables.name: Blood progesterone
variables.why: The placenta was the main source of progesterone in late pregnancy. Once it is delivered, the level falls within days.

variables.name: Mass of the uterus
variables.why: With estrogen and progesterone falling and the uterus contracting, the muscle cells break down their own proteins and shrink: uterine involution.

variables.name: Urine output
variables.why: The extra fluid of pregnancy moves back into the blood and is cleared by the kidneys, so she passes large volumes of urine in the first days.

variables.name: Number of myometrial cells
variables.why: Involution shrinks the existing muscle cells rather than removing them, so their number stays about the same.

why.correct: Suckling sends nerve signals to the hypothalamus and oxytocin is released. The uterus, still rich in oxytocin receptor proteins, contracts: these are afterpains. They speed uterine involution.
options: Prolactin acts on the milk-making cells of the breast, not the myometrium.
Correct. Oxytocin released by suckling contracts the uterus and helps it involute.
Dilation belongs to the first stage of labor. After birth the cervix closes.
Cramps timed to suckling point to oxytocin, not to retained tissue, which shows as heavy or prolonged bleeding.

why.correct: Prostaglandins from the fetal membranes and uterine lining contract the myometrium and soften the cervix, and oxytocin adds to their release. Blocking their synthesis weakens contractions and slows ripening.
options: Oxytocin comes from hypothalamic neurons ending in the posterior pituitary, not from prostaglandins.
Progesterone keeps the uterus quiet. If prostaglandins raised it, blocking them would speed labor, the opposite of what is seen.
Correct. Removing a signal that contracts the uterus and ripens the cervix delays labor.
Near term, gap junctions increase, coupling the cells. Closing them would quiet the uterus, so blocking prostaglandins would then speed labor, not delay it.

why.correct: In the labor loop, stretch of the cervix causes oxytocin release and stronger contractions, which cause more stretch. A response that amplifies its own stimulus is positive feedback.
options: Many negative feedback loops also use hormones as the efferent pathway, such as the glucose loops.
Holding a variable near a set point is what negative feedback does.
Most homeostatic loops involve several organs, whether positive or negative.
Correct. The loop amplifies the stretch instead of opposing it.

why.correct: Trials showed routine episiotomy does not protect against severe tears and heals no better. It is now reserved for specific reasons, such as speeding the birth of a baby in distress.
options: An episiotomy widens the opening, so if anything it speeds the birth. That is why it is still used when the baby needs to be born quickly.
Correct. The benefit claimed for routine use did not hold up in trials.
The perineum often stretches enough, and many births cause no tear or only a small one.
An episiotomy is done as the head is being born, in the expulsion stage.

why.correct: The cervix is the narrow lower end of the uterus. The dilation stage of labor thins and opens it to about 10 cm.
options: Correct. The cervix thins and dilates during stage 1.
The vagina lies below the cervix. It stretches during stage 2 but is not what dilates to 10 cm.
The fundus is the dome at the top of the uterus, where contractions are strongest.
The amnion is the membrane around the fetus and amniotic fluid, not part of the uterine wall.

why.correct: This is retraction. The upper muscle ends each contraction slightly shorter and thicker, so it draws the thin lower segment and the softened cervix upward around the head: effacement and dilation.
options: Cell division is far too slow to thicken a wall over hours. The cells change length, not number.
Fluid would not explain why the upper wall thickens while the lower wall thins at the same time.
Correct. Retraction: each shortening thickens the upper segment and pulls the lower segment and cervix up and open.
Receptor protein numbers set how strongly the muscle responds to oxytocin. They would not thin the lower wall while thickening the upper one.

why.correct: Lochia turns from red to pinkish-brown after about 3 or 4 days and can continue for weeks. The fundus drops about 1 cm a day and is barely felt above the pubic symphysis by about two weeks.
options: Lochia usually lasts four to six weeks; only its red phase ends after the first few days.
The fundus is near the navel on the first day and descends day by day. At day 10 it should be much lower.
Correct. Changing lochia and a shrinking uterus are signs of normal involution.
Retained tissue shows as heavy, bright red bleeding and a uterus that stays large, the opposite of what she describes.

why.correct: Breathing lowers pulmonary resistance, and clamping the cord raises systemic resistance and cuts umbilical return. Left-sided pressures rise above right, which closes the foramen ovale and reverses flow in the ductus arteriosus, while oxygen from the lungs raises arterial oxygen.

variables.name: Pulmonary vascular resistance
variables.why: Air stretches the lungs open, and rising oxygen relaxes the pulmonary arterioles, helped by nitric oxide.

variables.name: Blood flow through the lungs
variables.why: With resistance falling, far more of the right ventricle's output passes through the lungs instead of the ductus arteriosus.

variables.name: Left atrial pressure
variables.why: Much more blood returns from the lungs through the pulmonary veins into the left atrium.

variables.name: Right atrial pressure
variables.why: Clamping the cord stops the flow returning from the placenta through the umbilical vein, so less blood enters the right atrium.

variables.name: Right-to-left flow through the foramen ovale
variables.why: Left atrial pressure now exceeds right, which pushes the septum primum against the opening and closes it.

variables.name: Oxygen in the baby's arterial blood
variables.why: Blood now picks up oxygen in the lungs, and the shunts that mixed oxygen-poor blood into the aorta close.

why.correct: After birth the pressures are reversed, so an open ductus shunts blood left to right, from the aorta into the lungs. The lungs and left heart carry extra volume, and runoff from the aorta in diastole widens the pulse pressure.

variables.name: Blood flow through the lungs
variables.why: Aortic pressure is now higher than pulmonary pressure, so blood flows from the aorta through the ductus into the pulmonary trunk and adds to the right ventricle's output.
