variables.name: Volume returning to the left atrium and ventricle
variables.why: The extra blood sent to the lungs returns through the pulmonary veins to the left heart.

variables.name: Aortic diastolic pressure
variables.why: During diastole, blood keeps draining from the aorta into the lower-pressure pulmonary circuit through the ductus.

variables.name: Pulse pressure
variables.why: Diastolic pressure falls while the larger stroke volume keeps systolic pressure up, so the gap widens and pulses feel bounding.

why.correct: More blood returns from the lungs to the left atrium, and less returns to the right atrium once the cord is clamped. The higher left pressure pushes the septum primum against the rim of the opening, like a door pushed shut. Fusion comes months later.
options: Fusion of the flap to the wall happens over months, and in about one adult in four never happens. The quick closure is a pressure effect.
Oxygen-driven contraction closes the ductus arteriosus, a muscular vessel. The foramen ovale is a flap valve with no ring of muscle.
Correct. A pressure reversal between the atria presses the flap closed.
Falling prostaglandin E2 helps close the ductus arteriosus, not the foramen ovale.

why.correct: Oxygen makes the ductus smooth muscle contract, and losing prostaglandin E2 removes the signal that kept it open. With aortic pressure above pulmonary pressure, flow through the ductus reverses, so oxygen-rich aortic blood reaches its wall.
options: Correct. Rising oxygen contracts the ductus smooth muscle.
Correct. Prostaglandin E2 kept the ductus open before birth; its fall lets it close.
Pulmonary pressure falls after birth. A rise would favor flow from the pulmonary trunk into the aorta, as before birth.
Prostaglandin E2 keeps the ductus open. A prostaglandin infusion is used to keep it open on purpose.
Correct. With aortic pressure now above pulmonary pressure, flow reverses, and oxygen-rich aortic blood bathes the ductus wall, adding to the oxygen signal that constricts it.

why.correct: Prostaglandin E2 holds the ductus open, and preterm ducts are especially sensitive to it. Blocking prostaglandin synthesis with indomethacin or ibuprofen removes that signal, and the ductus constricts.
options: A prostaglandin infusion keeps the ductus open. It is used when a baby's heart defect makes the ductus the only route for blood.
Low oxygen relaxes the ductus. Rising oxygen is one of the signals that closes it.
Epinephrine raises heart rate and contractility. It has no role in closing the ductus.
Correct. Removing prostaglandin lets the ductus close.

why.correct: Prostaglandin E2 keeps the ductus open, so an infusion of a prostaglandin reopens or holds it open and restores blood flow to the lungs.
options: Oxygen constricts the ductus. Closing it faster would cut off the baby's only route to the lungs.
Correct. A prostaglandin infusion keeps the ductus open.
Blocking prostaglandins closes the ductus, which is the treatment for an unwanted open ductus, not for a baby who depends on it.
Cooling a newborn makes it burn brown fat, using more oxygen and glucose, and it does nothing for the ductus.

why.correct: The ductus arteriosus joins the pulmonary trunk to the aorta. Before birth it carries most of the right ventricle's output past the lungs; after birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
options: Correct. It links the pulmonary trunk and the aortic arch.
The foramen ovale is an opening between the two atria, inside the heart.
The ductus venosus is in the liver, linking the umbilical vein to the inferior vena cava.
The umbilical vein brings oxygen-rich blood from the placenta to the fetus's liver.

why.correct: The foramen ovale is the flap-covered opening between the atria through which blood crosses from right to left before birth.
options: The fossa ovalis is the shallow dip the foramen ovale leaves once its flap has fused. Before birth, the pinned opening is still open.
The ductus arteriosus is a vessel between the pulmonary trunk and aorta, outside the atria.
Correct. The foramen ovale links the right and left atria before birth.
The coronary sinus drains the heart's own veins into the right atrium. It does not connect the atria.

why.correct: The ductus venosus carries most of the umbilical vein's oxygen-rich blood past the liver into the inferior vena cava. After birth it closes and becomes the ligamentum venosum.
options: The hepatic portal vein carries blood from the intestines into the liver. It stays open for life.
The inferior vena cava is the large vein the ductus venosus empties into.
The umbilical arteries carry fetal blood to the placenta; they branch from arteries in the pelvis, not in the liver.
Correct. This shunt bypasses the liver before birth.

why.correct: After the ductus arteriosus constricts in the first days, it fills with fibrous tissue over the following weeks and becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.
options: The umbilical arteries become the medial umbilical ligaments on the abdominal wall.
The ductus venosus becomes the ligamentum venosum in the liver.
The foramen ovale leaves the fossa ovalis, a dip in the wall between the atria.
Correct. The ductus arteriosus becomes the ligamentum arteriosum.

why.correct: At 29 weeks, the type II cells have not yet made enough surfactant. Surface tension collapses alveoli at the end of each breath, so every breath must reopen them: respiratory distress syndrome.
options: Correct. Surfactant shortage causes respiratory distress syndrome in preterm babies.
An open ductus can add to lung problems later, but distress within the first hour in a very preterm baby points first to surfactant shortage.
Meconium in the fluid is a problem of term and post-term babies under stress, not of a baby born at 29 weeks.
Cold stress raises oxygen use and can worsen breathing, but it does not cause grunting and collapsing alveoli by itself.

why.correct: Grunting is breathing out against a partly closed glottis. It keeps some pressure in the airways at the end of each breath, so fewer alveoli collapse. Continuous positive airway pressure does the same thing from outside.
options: Only surfactant lowers surface tension. Grunting works by pressure, not chemistry.
Raising carbon dioxide would make the baby worse off. Grunting helps by keeping alveoli open, which improves gas exchange.
Grunting holds air in the lungs; it does not clear fluid from them.
Correct. The held pressure counters the collapse that surface tension causes.

why.correct: A glucocorticoid given to the mother crosses the placenta and speeds the baby's type II cells toward making surfactant, which cuts respiratory distress syndrome and newborn deaths.
options: Glucocorticoids do not stop contractions. Other drugs are used to delay preterm labor for a short time.
Rh sensitization is prevented with an injection of anti-D, an antibody, not a glucocorticoid.
Correct. It speeds surfactant production in the fetal lungs.
Closing the ductus before birth would be harmful, because the fetus needs it to send blood past its lungs.

why.correct: Each sign scores 1: color (body pink, hands and feet blue), pulse (below 100), grimace (a grimace only), activity (some bending) and respiration (slow, irregular). The total is 5, a moderately abnormal score.
options: Correct. Five signs at 1 point each gives 5.
A 7 would need two signs scoring 2, for example a heart rate of 100 or more and a strong cry.
A 4 would need one sign scoring 0, such as absent breathing or no response to stimulation.
A 6 would need one sign scoring 2, for example a heart rate of 100 or more.

why.correct: Meconium, the dark sticky contents of the fetal gut, is passed by nearly all term babies within 48 hours. Failure to pass it can mean a blockage or a problem with the intestine's movement, which needs investigating.
options: Correct. Delayed meconium points to a problem with the intestine.
Gut bacteria arrive during and after birth. Their absence would not stop meconium from being passed.
Meconium was formed before birth from swallowed fluid and shed cells, so it is passed even before feeding is established.
Meconium is normally passed in the first one to two days, not after a week.

why.correct: Cold skin signals the hypothalamus, sympathetic nerves release norepinephrine onto brown fat, and the brown fat burns fuel in mitochondria that release the energy as heat. That nonshivering thermogenesis uses oxygen and glucose fast, so a cold baby can become low in glucose and oxygen.
options: Newborns shiver weakly and get little heat from it. Their main heat source is brown fat.
Sympathetic activity in cold raises glucose release from the liver; it does not stop it. The fall comes from use outrunning supply.
Correct. Nonshivering thermogenesis costs oxygen and glucose.
Cold and sympathetic activity hold insulin release down, not up.

why.correct: Suckling stimulates mechanoreceptors, whose signals travel to the hypothalamus. Hypothalamic neurons release oxytocin from the posterior pituitary, and oxytocin in the blood makes the myoepithelial cells squeeze milk out of the alveoli into the ducts.
Dopamine holds prolactin back. Suckling makes the hypothalamus release less dopamine, which is what lets prolactin surge.
options: This step is right. Suckling is the stimulus, carried by afferent nerves.
This is the error. Dopamine release falls, removing the brake on prolactin.
This step is right. Prolactin rises once dopamine falls.
This step is right. The alveolar cells carry the prolactin receptor proteins.
This step is right. Prolactin's surge supports the milk for the following feed; oxytocin ejects the milk already made.

why.correct: Full milk production starts when progesterone falls after the placenta is delivered. Retained placental tissue keeps making progesterone, which keeps blocking prolactin's action, so the milk does not come in until the tissue is removed.
options: Correct. Placental progesterone keeps the brake on milk production.
Dopamine comes from the hypothalamus, not the placenta.
Oxytocin ejects milk; it does not make it. Prolactin, blocked by progesterone, is what is missing here.
Heavy bleeding can slow milk production, but the retained tissue explains the delay directly, through progesterone.

why.correct: It is one milk, made the same way. Fat droplets stick to the walls of the alveoli and small ducts, so the early milk out is lower in fat, and the fat is carried out as the breast is emptied.
options: Oxytocin ejects milk; it does not change what the cells make during a feed.
The same alveolar cells make all the milk. The difference comes from how fat moves out of the breast.
Correct. Fat content climbs as the breast empties.
Prolactin's surge supports milk for the next feed, not the milk flowing now.

why.correct: Most milk IgA is not absorbed. It works where it lands, on the baby's gut lining, binding microbes in the family's surroundings so they cannot attach: natural passive immunity.
options: The baby's main blood antibody in early life is IgG that crossed the placenta. Milk IgA mostly stays in the gut.
Borrowed antibody is passive immunity: it protects without switching on the baby's own B cells.
IgG is the antibody that crosses the placenta. IgA reaches the baby in milk after birth.
Correct. Milk IgA protects the mucous membrane of the gut.

why.correct: Her breasts were full, so milk had been made. Pain, fear and stress inhibit oxytocin release through the hypothalamus, so the myoepithelial cells did not contract and the milk was not ejected.
options: Correct. Stress blocks the oxytocin that ejects milk.
Prolactin makes milk, and her breasts were already full. The problem was getting the milk out.
Full breasts show that the alveolar cells had been making milk.
Less dopamine would raise prolactin; blocking dopamine would not stop milk from flowing.

why.correct: Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli: the milk ejection reflex.
options: Estrogen makes the ducts grow during pregnancy. It does not eject milk.
Correct. Oxytocin ejects milk.
Progesterone makes the alveoli multiply in pregnancy and holds back full milk production until it falls.
Human placental lactogen helps prepare the breast in pregnancy and falls after the placenta is delivered.

why.correct: Dopamine is the main brake on prolactin. A drug that acts like dopamine keeps prolactin low even when the breasts are stimulated, so milk production stops.
options: Correct. Mimicking dopamine suppresses prolactin, and with it milk production.
Dopamine lowers prolactin; a drug that acts like it cannot raise prolactin.
The drug acts on prolactin release from the anterior pituitary, not on oxytocin.
Oxytocin ejects milk, but prolactin is needed to make it.

why.correct: Bb means two different alleles of the gene, one on each homologous chromosome. Two different alleles make the person heterozygous.
options: Homozygous dominant would be BB, two copies of the dominant allele.
Correct. Two different alleles make a heterozygote.
Homozygous recessive would be bb, two copies of the recessive allele.
Hemizygous describes a single copy, as for genes on a male's one X chromosome. Bb has two copies.

why.correct: Both brothers carry the same genotype, but the diet kept phenylalanine low in one of them, so his brain developed normally. Phenotype is the result of genotype and environment together.
options: The question states both have the PKU genotype. The difference is in what they ate.
PKU is recessive, and dominance would not explain why the same genotype gave two outcomes.
Diet cannot change the alleles in a person's cells. It changed how the genotype was expressed as phenotype.
Correct. Same genotype, different phenotype, because of the diet.

why.correct: Each carrier (Cc) makes C and c gametes equally. The Punnett square gives 1 CC : 2 Cc : 1 cc, and only cc has the disease: 1 in 4.
options: 1 in 2 is the chance that a child is a carrier (Cc), not that the child is affected.
3 in 4 is the chance that a child is healthy.
Correct. One box in four is cc.
Healthy carriers each hide one disease allele, and a child who gets both has the disease, so the chance is not zero.

why.correct: The square gives CC, Cc, Cc and cc. The daughter is healthy, so she is not cc; that leaves three equally likely boxes, two of which are Cc. Her chance of being a carrier is 2 in 3.
options: 1 in 4 is the chance of being affected, which she is not.
1 in 2 is a carrier's share of all four boxes. Once you know she is healthy, the affected box is removed.
Correct. Two of the three healthy boxes are carriers.
3 in 4 is the chance of being healthy for any child before you know the outcome.

why.correct: Gametes are formed fresh for every pregnancy, and each pregnancy is an independent draw. The 1 in 4 applies to each child, whatever happened before.
options: Earlier children do not use up the risk. Each pregnancy starts again at 1 in 4.
There is no reason for the risk to change after one affected child; the parents' genotypes are the same.
Correct. The chance is 1 in 4 for every child of two carriers.
1 in 2 is the chance of a carrier child, not an affected one.

why.correct: The affected parent is Nn and the other nn. Two of the four boxes are Nn, and with a dominant allele one copy causes the disease, so each child has a 1 in 2 chance.
options: 1 in 4 would fit two heterozygous carriers of a recessive disease, not this cross.
3 in 4 would need two affected heterozygous parents (Nn × Nn), each passing N half the time.
Correct. Half the boxes are Nn.
Every child would be affected only if the affected parent were NN, which would give N in every gamete.

why.correct: Three boxes show the dominant phenotype: AA, Aa and Aa. Knowing the child shows it removes the aa box, and two of the remaining three are Aa, so the chance is 2 in 3.
options: 1 in 4 is the share of aa among all four boxes.
Correct. Two of the three dominant-phenotype boxes are heterozygous.
1 in 2 is the share of Aa among all four boxes, before you know the child's phenotype.
3 in 4 is the chance of the dominant phenotype, not of being heterozygous.

why.correct: The father (AB) gives either A or B; the mother (OO) always gives O. The children are AO (type A) or BO (type B), each with a 1 in 2 chance.
options: Correct. An A from the father with O from the mother gives AO, type A.
Correct. A B from the father with O from the mother gives BO, type B.
Type AB needs an A and a B allele. The mother can pass only O, so no child can get both.
Type O needs two O alleles. The father has none to give.

why.correct: Type A can be AO and type B can be BO. If each parent passes the O allele, the child is OO, type O. From an AO × BO cross, each child has a 1 in 4 chance of type O.
options: A type B father who is BO can pass on O. The blood types fit him being the father.
Blood type is set by the genotype and does not change after birth.
Correct. Two heterozygous parents can each pass on the recessive O allele.
O is recessive, not dominant. It shows only when a child has two O alleles.

why.correct: Both alleles are fully expressed side by side: the A enzyme and the B enzyme both work, and both antigens appear. That is codominance.
options: Incomplete dominance gives an intermediate phenotype. Here each allele's full product appears, not a blend.
The ABO gene is on an autosome, and the pattern is the same in both sexes.
ABO type is set by one gene with three alleles, not by many genes of small effect.
Correct. Both alleles show fully in the heterozygote.

why.correct: At the level of hemoglobin molecules the alleles are codominant; at the level of red cell sickling, the heterozygote is in between; at the level of disease, the sickle allele is recessive. Dominance describes a relationship for one phenotype.
options: Being expressed is not the same as being dominant. The heterozygote has no disease, so for disease the sickle allele is recessive.
Correct. Each level of phenotype shows a different pattern.
Both alleles are expressed at the molecule level, but the heterozygote has no disease, so the pattern is not codominant for disease.
The hemoglobin gene is on an autosome, and the trait occurs equally in both sexes.

why.correct: A son gets his X from his mother and his Y from his father. The carrier mother passes her hemophilia X to half her children, so each son has a 1 in 2 chance of being affected.
options: Correct. A son's only X comes from his carrier mother, who passes the allele half the time.
1 in 4 is the chance for any child of either sex, since only sons can be affected here. For a son it is 1 in 2.
The father's normal clotting does not protect a son, because a son gets no X from his father.
The mother has one normal X as well, which she passes to half her sons.

why.correct: The father gives his X, with the hemophilia allele, to every daughter and his Y to every son. Daughters get a normal X from their mother too, so they are carriers; sons get their X from their noncarrier mother, so they are unaffected.
options: That is the pattern for a carrier mother and an unaffected father, the reverse of this family.
A son receives his father's Y, not his X, so the father cannot pass hemophilia to his sons.
Correct. Father-to-daughter passing makes all daughters carriers; sons are spared.
Half of all children affected describes an autosomal dominant allele, not an X-linked recessive one.

why.correct: Males have one X, so a single recessive allele shows in them. Carrier mothers pass it to half their sons, and an affected man passes it to all daughters, who are carriers, so it can reappear in their sons, skipping a generation.
options: Correct. One copy is enough in males, two are needed in females.
Correct. Carrier mothers pass the allele to half their sons.
A father gives his son a Y, not an X, so father-to-son passing rules out X-linked inheritance.
Every child affected is not typical of any single-gene pattern here; an affected man's sons are unaffected.
Correct. An affected man's daughters are carriers, and their sons can be affected.

why.correct: The genes for the red and green cone pigments are on the X chromosome. A male has no second X to mask a faulty allele, while a female is color blind only if both her X chromosomes carry one.
options: Correct. One X in males versus two in females explains the difference.
The Y carries few genes, and not these. Color blindness passes from mothers to sons, not fathers to sons.
Hormones do not repair cone pigments. The difference is in the number of X chromosomes.
The allele behaves the same way in both sexes; males simply have no second copy.

why.correct: A dominant lethal allele can persist only if it acts late or keeps arising by new mutation. Huntington symptoms usually start between 30 and 50, after many people have already had children, each with a 1 in 2 chance of inheriting it.
options: Correct. Late onset lets the allele pass to the next generation before it causes harm.
With a dominant allele there are no healthy carriers: one copy eventually causes the disease.
Huntington disease is autosomal and dominant in both sexes.
Dominance does not make an allele more common. Its frequency depends on survival and reproduction, not on dominance.

why.correct: Maternal age raises the risk of chromosome-number errors because oocytes wait decades in meiosis I and the proteins holding their chromosomes together weaken. It does not change the 1 in 4 risk from two carriers of a recessive allele.

variables.name: Chance of nondisjunction in her oocytes
variables.why: Her oocytes have been paused in meiosis I for 15 more years, and the proteins holding their paired chromosomes together have weakened further.

variables.name: Risk of a child with trisomy 21
variables.why: More nondisjunction gives more oocytes with an extra chromosome 21, raising the risk from about 1 in 1,200 to about 1 in 100.

variables.name: Chance that a child of hers and a carrier partner has cystic fibrosis, if she is a carrier
variables.why: Segregation of a single gene's alleles is 1 in 2 per gamete at any age, so two carriers still face a 1 in 4 chance.

variables.name: Number of chromosomes in her body cells
variables.why: Her own body cells stay at 46; age affects the separation of chromosomes in oocytes, not her karyotype.

why.correct: Cells must be dividing to condense their chromosomes. Stopping them in metaphase catches the chromosomes at their most condensed, staining reveals the bands, and arranging them in pairs by size, centromere position and banding gives the karyotype.
An egg with 24 chromosomes joined by a normal sperm with 23 gives 47, with three copies of chromosome 21: trisomy 21.
options: This step is right. The oocyte waits in meiosis I from before the mother's birth until ovulation.
This step is right. The proteins are not replaced, so they weaken with age.
This step is right. That is nondisjunction in meiosis I.
This step is right. The egg now has one extra chromosome.
This is the error. 24 + 23 = 47, not 45. A zygote with 45 would come from an egg missing a chromosome.

why.correct: Polygenic traits depend on many genes, each adding a small effect, plus environmental factors such as nutrition. Adding up many small effects gives a continuous, bell-shaped spread.
options: Codominance involves two alleles of one gene both showing, which gives a few distinct types, not a smooth range.
Correct. Many genes of small effect give a bell curve.
An X-linked trait follows one gene on the X and shows sex differences in who is affected.
A recessive lethal allele kills homozygotes; it does not produce a continuous range.

why.correct: With thousands of variants each adding or subtracting a little, most people inherit a mix of both kinds, and few inherit mostly one kind. That puts most people near the middle and few at the extremes.
options: Dominance describes one gene's alleles. It does not explain why a trait shaped by thousands of variants clusters around the middle.
A single gene with two alleles gives two or three distinct types, not a smooth range.
Environment matters, but genes still matter: tall parents tend to have tall children.
Correct. Many small effects in both directions give a bell-shaped spread.

why.correct: This is translocation Down syndrome. It does not depend on maternal age, and it can be inherited from a parent who carries the rearrangement without symptoms. If a parent carries it, the risk in later pregnancies is much higher than the age-based risk.
options: Correct. A parent may be a balanced carrier of the translocation.
The age-based risk applies to Down syndrome from nondisjunction. A translocation may come from a parent, which can raise the risk sharply.
Cystic fibrosis is a single-gene disease and has nothing to do with this karyotype.
Translocation Down syndrome is not tied to maternal age, so her age does not set her risk.

why.correct: 47 chromosomes, sex chromosomes XY (male), and +21 marks the extra chromosome 21: trisomy 21, Down syndrome.
options: Correct. XY is male, and +21 is the extra chromosome.
XY means male; a female would be XX.
A missing chromosome would give 45, not 47.
An extra X would read 47,XXY. Here the extra chromosome is number 21.

why.correct: At B the capacity curve sits between the two dashed lines. It still covers resting needs, so resting values are normal, but it no longer reaches the level a major stress demands. That shrinking gap is loss of reserve.
options: Correct. Reserve, the gap between capacity and need, has closed for a major stress but not for rest.
The curve at B is well above the resting line, which is why resting tests are normal.
The resting line is flat across all ages. What changes is capacity.
Capacity at B is about 55% of peak, compared with 100% at A.

why.correct: The solid capacity curve crosses the upper dashed line, at 60% of peak, at about age 75. After that, a major stress asks for more than the body can deliver.
options: At 30 capacity is at its peak, 100%, far above the stress line.
At 50 capacity is still about 85%, above the stress line.
Correct. The curve crosses the stress line at about 75.
The curve does cross the stress line, although it never falls below the resting line on this graph.

why.correct: DNA polymerase needs a primer and adds nucleotides to one end only. The gap left by the last primer at a chromosome tip cannot be filled, so a little of the end is lost each division. Telomerase could add repeats back, but most body cells make almost none.
options: Oxidative damage can speed telomere loss, but the loss at every division comes from the copying machinery itself.
Telomerase adds repeats; it lengthens telomeres.
Apoptosis kills the whole cell. It does not trim chromosome ends in a dividing cell.
Correct. This is the end-replication problem, uncorrected without telomerase.

why.correct: Germ cells use telomerase, so each generation starts with long telomeres. Most cancers switch it back on, which lets them divide without limit. Stem cells use a little, which slows but does not stop their telomere loss.
options: Correct. Germ cells make telomerase.
Correct. Most cancer cells reactivate telomerase.
Ordinary body cells such as fibroblasts make almost no telomerase, which is why they reach a division limit.
Senescent cells have stopped dividing, often because their telomeres became too short.
Correct. Stem cells make a small amount.

why.correct: Without telomerase, telomeres shorten with each division until their caps fail. The cell reads the bare ends as damaged DNA, checkpoint proteins such as p53 stop the cycle, and more and more cells become senescent: the Hayflick limit.

variables.name: Average telomere length
variables.why: Each division loses a little of every chromosome end through the end-replication problem, and nothing adds it back.

variables.name: Number of divisions the cells have left
variables.why: As telomeres approach the length at which their caps fail, fewer divisions remain before the Hayflick limit.

variables.name: Checkpoint activity, such as p53
variables.why: Short telomeres with failed caps are read as damaged DNA, which activates p53 and other checkpoint proteins.

variables.name: Share of cells in senescence
variables.why: Cells whose checkpoints have stopped the cycle for good stay alive but no longer divide.

why.correct: Stopping division for good prevents a cell with damaged DNA from becoming cancerous. But senescent cells stay active, releasing cytokines and protein-digesting enzymes that inflame and damage their neighbors, and they accumulate with age.
options: Senescent cells do not divide, so they slow repair; they do not speed it.
Correct. Tumor protection is the benefit; inflammatory secretions are the cost.
Senescence does not lengthen telomeres; short telomeres are one of its triggers. It protects against cancer.
That describes apoptosis, the other outcome of a checkpoint. A senescent cell stays alive.

why.correct: Immune responses weaken with age, and the fever response is often blunted, so an older adult with a serious infection may have a normal temperature and show confusion instead.
options: Pneumonia usually does cause fever in younger adults. The missing fever here reflects his age.
The hypothalamic set point does not rise with age; if anything, older adults run slightly cooler.
The confusion is caused by the infection, not the other way round, and it does not lower temperature.
Correct. Blunted fever is common in older adults with infection.

why.correct: A stiffer aorta raises systolic pressure and widens pulse pressure; the SA node and sympathetic response decline, lowering maximum heart rate; and a thicker, stiffer left ventricle fills more slowly early in diastole, so atrial contraction matters more.
options: Correct. A stiff aorta cannot absorb each stroke volume, so systolic pressure rises.
Correct. Systolic rises while diastolic stays level or falls.
Correct. Maximum heart rate falls by roughly 0.7 to 1 beat per minute a year.
Resting cardiac output changes little in healthy aging. What falls is maximal output, the reserve.
Correct. The stiffer ventricle fills less early in diastole.

why.correct: A young, elastic aorta stretches as the ventricle ejects, blunting the systolic rise, and recoils in diastole, holding diastolic pressure up. A stiff aorta does neither, so systolic pressure rises and diastolic pressure stays level or falls.
options: Correct. Lost elasticity widens the pulse pressure.
Stroke volume does not rise much with age. The pattern comes from the stiff arterial wall.
Relaxed arterioles would lower resistance and both pressures, not raise systolic alone.
Blood does not become thinner with age, and lower viscosity would lower pressure, not raise systolic.

why.correct: Stiffer arteries stretch less, so baroreceptors signal the fall in pressure weakly, and the heart responds less to sympathetic signals. The reflex that normally raises heart rate and constricts vessels on standing is slow and small, so pressure falls: orthostatic hypotension.
options: Correct. A weak, slow baroreceptor reflex lets pressure fall on standing.
Aldosterone falls with age, and extra aldosterone would expand blood volume and protect against a fall.
The SA node loses cells and slows its maximum rate with age; a faster node would help, not harm.
Venous valves weaken with age, if anything; stronger valves would help return blood when standing.

why.correct: Plasma creatinine depends on how much is made as well as how fast it is cleared. With little muscle she makes little creatinine, so even a reduced GFR keeps the level normal. eGFR corrects for age and sex and reveals the loss of nephrons.
options: Creatinine is cleared mainly by filtration, and nothing speeds its secretion with age.
Creatinine is filtered freely at any age; less of it is filtered only because GFR is lower.
Correct. Low production offsets low clearance, masking the fall in GFR.
eGFR includes age and sex, which is exactly why it is used to reveal the fall in GFR.

why.correct: Nephrons are lost with age, so GFR and the clearance of renally excreted drugs fall. Less body water also concentrates water-soluble drugs. The same dose gives higher levels, which is why doses are lowered for older adults.
options: GFR falls with age; it does not rise.
The level depends on how fast the drug is cleared as well as on the dose.
Older cells still carry receptor proteins; older adults often respond more strongly to drugs, not less.
Correct. Slower clearance raises the drug level.

why.correct: Without telomerase, each division shortens the telomeres until one loses its cap. The bare end looks like broken DNA, checkpoint proteins arrest the cell permanently, and the surviving senescent cell releases inflammatory cytokines and enzymes that damage its neighbors.
Estrogen restrains osteoclasts. When it falls, osteoclasts become more active, so resorption speeds up.
options: This step is right. Menopause ends ovarian estrogen production.
This step is right. Estrogen normally holds osteoclast activity down.
This is the error. Estrogen restrains osteoclasts; losing it makes them more active, not less.
This step is right. More resorption than formation means net bone loss.
This step is right. Spongy bone's large surface lets it lose mass fastest.

why.correct: Fast glycolytic fibers make quick, powerful contractions. They atrophy most with age, and some are lost when their motor neurons die, so power falls more than endurance.
options: Slow oxidative fibers are relatively spared, which is why endurance holds up better than power.
Correct. Fast glycolytic fibers shrink most.
Sarcopenia is the loss of skeletal muscle, not cardiac muscle.
Sarcopenia describes skeletal muscle, not smooth muscle.

why.correct: A new antigen needs naive T cells that happen to fit it. The thymus shrinks from puberty on and makes few new naive T cells, so the T cell pool fills with memory cells from past infections and fewer naive clones are available. B cell responses weaken too.
options: Memory cells from past infections persist and come to dominate the T cell pool. The shortage is of naive cells.
Correct. Fewer naive T cells means a narrower, weaker response to new antigens.
Antibodies bind antigens normally; fewer and weaker new antibodies are made.
Vaccines still reach the lymph nodes. The response there is what is weaker.

why.correct: The lens stiffens in everyone with age, so near focus fails from the mid-40s. Dementia, anemia and incontinence all become more common with age but are diseases with causes to look for.
options: Correct. Presbyopia happens to everyone as the lens stiffens.
Dementia becomes more common with age but is a disease; most older adults do not have it.
Resting blood counts stay normal in healthy aging, so anemia has a cause to find.
Incontinence is common but not normal, and it often has a treatable cause.

why.correct: Fewer sweat glands make heat harder to shed; blunted thirst means he did not drink enough; and kidneys that concentrate urine less well keep losing water. Together they let water loss and body temperature climb until sodium rose and his brain was affected.
options: Each of these changes goes the wrong way: sweat glands decrease, thirst is blunted and the kidneys conserve water less well.
The temperature set point does not rise with age, and more ADH would conserve water, not lose it.
Correct. Several systems each lose reserve, and the losses add up.
Subcutaneous fat falls with age, and metabolic rate falls rather than rises.

why.correct: Each system loses capacity through its own mechanism: fewer pacemaker cells and weaker sympathetic response in the heart, lost elastic recoil in the lungs, lost nephrons in the kidneys, net resorption in bone and a shrinking thymus in the immune system. Resting function is kept, but reserve falls everywhere.

variables.name: Maximum heart rate
variables.why: The SA node loses pacemaker cells and responds less to sympathetic stimulation, so the highest rate falls by roughly 0.7 to 1 beat a year.

variables.name: Residual volume
variables.why: Loss of lung elastic recoil lets small airways close earlier during expiration, trapping more air.

variables.name: Glomerular filtration rate
variables.why: Nephrons are lost with age, reducing the total filtering surface.

variables.name: Bone mass
variables.why: After about 30, osteoclasts resorb slightly more than osteoblasts rebuild in each remodeling cycle.

variables.name: Naive T cells in the blood
variables.why: The thymus shrinks from puberty on and makes few new naive T cells.

why.correct: Near focus needs the lens to round up when the zonule fibers go slack. The lens keeps adding cells and stiffens with age, so it cannot round up enough: presbyopia.
options: Correct. A stiff lens cannot accommodate for near objects.
The cornea's shape changes little with age and cannot explain the loss of near focus.
Losing cones would dull color and sharp vision, not near focus, which depends on the lens.
The pupil gets smaller with age, which, if anything, sharpens focus a little.

why.correct: Each new hair gets its color from melanocytes in the follicle, replenished from a pool of pigment stem cells. As that pool runs out, new hairs grow without melanin and look gray or white.
options: Graying reflects missing melanin in new hairs, not a change in the keratin of old ones.
Sweat glands have nothing to do with hair color.
Scalp blood flow continues; hairs still grow, just without pigment.
Correct. Without melanocytes, new hairs grow without pigment.

why.correct: Oxidative damage contributes to aging, but reactive oxygen species also act as normal signals, and large trials of vitamin E and beta-carotene did not slow aging or prevent chronic disease. Beta-carotene raised lung cancer in smokers.
options: Supplements do not stop oxidative damage inside cells in any measurable way that slows aging, and trials have not shown a benefit.
Oxidative damage is one contributor to aging; it is just not the single cause.
Correct. The trials were negative, and some showed harm.
No antioxidant has been shown to lengthen telomeres in all cells. Telomerase is what adds repeats.

why.correct: Older muscle responds less than young muscle but still grows and strengthens under load, and nerve activation improves too. Much of the weakness blamed on age is disuse that training can reverse.
options: The residents had lost muscle and strength; the point is that training restored much of it.
Correct. Resistance training works at any age.
Training enlarges existing fibers; it does not build whole new muscles.
Better nerve activation contributes early, but the fibers also grow with training.
